title: Guacamole
subtitle: Fresh avocado dip with lime, coriander, and jalapeño
excerpt: Ripe avocados mashed with lime juice, red onion, coriander, jalapeño, and tomato. The right texture depends on which avocados you use and how much you mash them. This recipe covers how to choose ripe avocados and how to make a dip that holds together.
sourceNotes: Guacamole: a dip with pre-Columbian origins, documented in Aztec sources from the 16th century. The modern version served with chips and as a Tex-Mex condiment became a US restaurant staple by the 1970s. The recipe here follows the Tex-Mex tradition with red onion, jalapeño, tomato, coriander, and lime. Based on classic American and Mexican published sources.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make guacamole no more than 2 hours before serving. Press cling film directly onto the surface to exclude air. Stir before serving. The lime juice slows browning but does not prevent it entirely.

content.text: Guacamole starts with the avocados. For this recipe, they need to be fully ripe: yielding to gentle pressure all over, with no firm spots. An underripe avocado mashes into waxy, tasteless paste; an overripe one is grey and bitter. The lime juice goes in first to stop oxidisation as you work. Mash with a fork rather than a processor for a rough, chunky texture that's far better than a smooth purée.

items.prepNote: fully ripe: flesh should give under gentle pressure with no firm spots
seeds removed for less heat, finely chopped
seeds and liquid squeezed out, finely diced
finely chopped, leaves and tender stems
crushed to a paste with salt, optional

content.text: Dice the red onion very finely and rinse under cold water for 30 seconds, then squeeze dry. This removes the raw bite without losing the flavour.
Halve the avocados and remove the stones. Scoop the flesh into a bowl. Add the lime juice straight away and a generous pinch of salt.
Mash with a fork until roughly broken down. Leave some chunks. Guacamole should have texture, not be a smooth purée.
Add the rinsed red onion, jalapeño, diced tomato, and coriander. Fold through gently. Add the crushed garlic if using. Taste and adjust with more lime juice and salt.
Serve immediately, or press cling film directly onto the surface and refrigerate for up to 2 hours.

items.cause: Oxidisation: avocado flesh reacts with air
items.fix: The lime juice slows but does not stop browning. Press cling film directly onto the surface so no air touches it. If the top layer browns, scrape it off; the guacamole underneath stays green.

items.symptom: Watery pool forming at the bottom
items.cause: Tomato not de-seeded, or onion not squeezed dry
items.fix: Halve the tomato and squeeze out the seeds and liquid before dicing. Rinse and squeeze the red onion dry. Both add significant moisture if left untreated.

items.symptom: Tastes flat despite all the ingredients
items.cause: Under-salted, or not enough lime juice
items.fix: Salt and lime juice are the most important flavourings. Add more of both and taste again. The amount needed varies with the size and ripeness of the avocados.

items.cause: Onion too large-cut or not rinsed
items.fix: Dice the onion very finely, with no piece larger than 3 mm. Rinse under cold water and squeeze dry before adding. This removes pungency without losing the flavour.

content.text: Guacamole has been made in Mexico for at least 500 years. The Aztec word ahuacamolli, meaning avocado sauce, appears in Spanish colonial records from the 16th century. The Tex-Mex version with lime, coriander, jalapeño, and tomato became a US restaurant staple in the 1960s and 1970s. It is now one of the most-eaten dips in Britain and the standard side for any Tex-Mex meal.
